analysis.one_liner: Caps interest rates on consumer loans at 36%, extending protections now given only to service members.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 10 Democratic senators, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend the interest-rate cap and lending rules that already protect active-duty service members under the Military Lending Act to every consumer. That means a national 36% cap on annual percentage rates for consumer loans, fees rolled into that rate calculation, and the Military Lending Act's penalties and court remedies. High-cost products like payday loans, which often carry annual rates in the hundreds of percent, would effectively be shut down nationwide.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who currently turn to payday loans, auto title loans, and other high-cost credit when money runs short. Anyone who borrows under the bill would owe no more than 36% APR, and lenders charging more would owe the same penalties that apply under the Military Lending Act, with state attorneys general and regulators able to sue violators for three years after an offense. Service members already have these protections; the bill would give the same shield to veterans and everyone else.

how_it_helps.text: Applies the Military Lending Act's rules — including its 36% cap on the interest rate for consumer credit — to every creditor lending to any consumer, not just to service members and their families.

Counts fees the way the Defense Department's Military Lending Act rules do: for credit cards and other open-end credit, the APR must include charges like credit insurance premiums and fees for add-on ancillary products, closing the common workaround of hiding the real cost in fees.

Gives borrowers real teeth: creditors who violate the cap face the Military Lending Act's penalties and remedies, and state attorneys general and state regulators can sue violators in federal or state court within three years of a violation.
Blocks the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau from waiving the protections, requires the bureau to write rules within one year, and makes the cap effective no later than 18 months after enactment.
Lets states keep stronger protections: the bill does not preempt any state law that protects consumers more than the 36% federal cap.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders whose business models depend on rates above 36% — payday lenders, auto title lenders, and high-rate installment lenders — would lose the core of their national business. Credit card issuers and banks would face tighter treatment of fees like credit insurance and add-on products. Some high-risk borrowers who cannot qualify for credit at 36% or less would lose access to the credit they use today, unless alternatives such as credit union loans fill the gap.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: a 36% cap eliminates most payday and title lending as it exists, and borrowers with poor credit who today take a two-week loan at a triple-digit annual rate may find no lender at all — the price cap only helps people who can get a loan under it. Supporters would answer that the same cap has applied to service members since the Military Lending Act passed, and that credit unions are exempt and already offer small loans within the cap.

The bill carves out major credit markets: residential mortgages, loans to buy a car or other personal property when the loan finances that purchase, and loans from federal credit unions are all exempt from the 36% cap, so high-cost auto and mortgage credit would continue untouched.

Households that genuinely need emergency cash would still need somewhere to turn; the bill caps the price of credit but does not itself create an alternative source of small-dollar credit for people banks decline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and well-tested: the bill copies, word for key part, a rate-cap and fee-disclosure regime that Congress already applied to service members, and it preserves stronger state laws rather than overriding them. The real cost falls on borrowers whose credit profiles do not clear a 36% underwriting bar — for them the bill removes a product without guaranteeing a replacement, though federal credit unions are exempt and can lawfully make small loans under the cap. On balance it is a strong consumer protection with a genuine, but bounded, access-to-credit tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley, joined by Senators Sherrod Brown, Jack Reed, and Chris Van Hollen, introduced the Veterans and Consumers Fair Credit Act in the Senate on November 12, 2019.
That same day the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs — the furthest it ever got.
Nine additional Democratic senators cosponsored the bill, but the Banking Committee held no hearing, took no vote, and never reported the bill to the Senate floor for the rest of the Congress.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and bills not passed die when a Congress ends; the 36% national cap was never enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, auto title, and other lenders charging more than 36% APR keep their national market, and the Senate committee majority never had to record a vote on the cap.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-rate lenders kept the status quo

against.name: Payday and high-cost lending industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending the Military Lending Act's 36% rate cap to all consumers, which would outlaw their core products.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 Senate supporters were Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored, and the bill never left the Banking Committee, which Republicans chaired in the 116th Congress.

industries.industry: Payday, auto title, and high-rate installment lenders
industries.note: A 36% national APR cap would make their core products — loans priced at annual rates of several hundred percent — illegal for all borrowers. These lenders profit by charging struggling households the highest rates in consumer credit, so their interest runs directly against the borrowers the bill protects.

Most credit card APRs sit below 36%, but the bill counts credit insurance premiums and fees for add-on ancillary products toward the cap and applies the Military Lending Act's penalties, raising compliance stakes on fee-heavy cards. The hit is modest for mainstream issuers but real for subprime card portfolios.
The bill exempts federal credit unions subject to their existing statutory usury limit, letting them serve borrowers who leave high-cost lenders. Their interest runs alongside the public's.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and dealer-arranged auto financing
industries.note: The bill expressly excludes residential mortgages and purchase-money loans for cars and personal property, leaving those markets — including dealer add-on fees and financing markups — outside the cap. The carve-out preserves the current, higher-cost structure of those markets.
